claims.text: Ab initio-informed machine-learning potentials can explicitly represent point defects and oxygen impurities in a bulk HfNbTaTiZr transport simulation.
The proposed framework will predict bulk HfNbTaTiZr electrical conductivity within ±10% of experiment over approximately 0–200 K.
The proposed framework will predict bulk HfNbTaTiZr electrical conductivity within ±10% of experiment over approximately 300–1200 K.
The ±10% accuracy target applies to both defect-free and 1 wt.% oxygen-containing specimens.
The proposed framework will be more accurate than conventional analytical models based on perfect-crystal approximations.
The initial computational reference is an ideal, single-phase, defect-free HfNbTaTiZr crystal.
The proposed comparison includes defect-free and oxygen-containing specimens in both stated temperature regimes.
Point defects and oxygen atoms act as transport-scattering centers in HfNbTaTiZr.
Point defects and oxygen alter electron-transport pathways.
Point defects and oxygen alter phonon-transport pathways.
Explicit defect physics captures scattering processes omitted by idealized perfect-crystal models.
Oxygen impurities induce localized states that modify electrical conduction.
Representing defect and impurity effects will bridge the discrepancy between idealized calculations and experiments at both low and high temperatures.
Conventional analytical approaches generally assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
Conventional analytical predictions typically differ from measured conductivity by more than ±10% when defects or oxygen impurities are present.
The proposed model is expected to be applicable only within 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Outside the specified temperature intervals, unmodeled quantum or diffusion effects may reduce accuracy.
Defect clustering and temperature-dependent dynamic effects may limit quantitative accuracy.
A deviation greater than ±10% in either temperature regime for either specimen type is defined as a falsifying result.
